questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
questions.solution: The image is of stormwater being (1) ___ INTO the sea — the wasted resource. 'Flush ... into' is the natural verb of wasted flow; drink, sell and freeze cannot take 'into the sea' meaningfully.
questions.passage: India's urban water crisis is less about rainfall than about planning. Every monsoon, cities (1) ___ millions of litres of stormwater into the sea, and by April the same cities queue for water (2) ___ by tankers from distant reservoirs. Rooftop harvesting, compulsory on paper in many states, is ignored in practice because builders treat it as an (3) ___ expense. The cost of this neglect is (4) ___ every summer: borewells fail, tanker prices triple, and residents march to municipal offices. The remedy demands no new technology, only the discipline to enforce rules that already (5) ___.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
questions.solution: The blank follows 'water' and precedes 'by tankers' — a reduced passive: water (which is) **carried** by tankers. The active form 'carry' would make 'water carry by tankers', which is ungrammatical.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
questions.solution: The blank sits between 'an' and 'expense' — an adjective is needed. 'An avoidable expense' = a cost that could be skipped, matching 'ignored in practice'. The other three are verb forms and leave the sentence without an adjective.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4).
questions.solution: 'The cost of this neglect is ___' needs a complement adjective after 'is': **visible**. 'Visibly' is an adverb and cannot follow 'is'; vision and visibility are nouns that clash with 'the cost ... is'.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5).
questions.solution: 'Rules that already ___' — the relative clause needs a finite present verb: rules that already **exist**. Existed would break the present-time frame ('demands ... to enforce'); existence and existing are not finite verbs.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

LETHARGIC
questions.solution: Lethargic means drowsy and without energy — **sluggish**. Cheerful and alert are near-opposites; honest is unrelated.
questions.shortcut: lethargy = lack of energy → sluggish.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

OPTIMIST
questions.solution: An optimist expects the best; the opposite person-type is a **pessimist**. Nationalist and ideal are not person-opposites; optimism is the same family noun, not the opposite person.
questions.shortcut: Opti- (best) vs pes- (worst): the pair is optimist–pessimist.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

To burn one's fingers
options: to suffer because of a hasty involvement
questions.solution: The picture: a hand poked into a fire too quickly gets scorched — **to suffer loss from acting rashly**, usually in money matters. The literal burn options are photographable decoys.
questions.shortcut: Hasty hand → hasty involvement → burnt fingers.

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution: Vacuum has **double u** — vac-uum — from Latin 'vacuus' (empty). Each distractor drops or moves one of the two u's.
questions.shortcut: vac + uum: two u's in a row.

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution: Liaison keeps the first **i** even though it is silent in speech: lia-ison (French 'lier', to bind). Liason drops it; Liaision doubles it.
questions.shortcut: liaison: l-i-a-i-s-o-n — count the two i's.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate one word for the given expression.

A place where money is coined
questions.solution: Coins are manufactured at a **mint**. A vault stores valuables; a treasury stores state money; a stall sells goods — none of them coins money.
questions.shortcut: mint = make coins (as in 'a mint-new coin').

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The manager was angry ___ the delay in the shipment.
questions.solution: 'Angry **about**' takes a thing or situation (the delay); 'angry with' takes a person. From, into and beneath are not collocations of angry.
questions.shortcut: angry with a person, angry about a thing.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The meeting was called ___ because of the strike.
questions.solution: 'Call off' = cancel. Call out (summon workers to strike), call in (invite) and call up (phone) do not fit 'because of the strike' cancelling the meeting.
questions.shortcut: call off = cancel.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

The news (a) are spreading (b) very fast (c) No error (d)
questions.solution: 'News' is a singular uncountable noun despite its -s ending: 'The news **is** spreading very fast.' The error is in part (b).
questions.shortcut: News, mathematics, physics — -s form, singular verb.

questions.q:
Select the part of the sentence that has an error.

I met (a) an European (b) at the party (c) No error (d)
questions.solution: 'European' begins with the consonant sound 'y' (yu-), so it takes **a**, not 'an': 'a European.' The article must follow sound, not spelling.
questions.shortcut: Article follows the SOUND: yu-ropean → a.

questions.q:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the sentence.

He don't know the answer to this question.
questions.solution: Third-person singular needs **does not**: 'He does not know.' B breaks the verb form; C wrongly makes a stative verb continuous; D accepts the error.
questions.shortcut: he/she/it + does not + V1.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The farmers are harvesting the crop.
options: The crop is being harvested by the farmers.
The crop is harvested by the farmers.
The crop was being harvested by the farmers.
The crop has been harvested by the farmers.
questions.solution: Present continuous → **is/are being + V3**; the new subject 'the crop' is singular → is being harvested. B drops the continuous; C shifts to past; D shifts to perfect.
questions.shortcut: are harvesting → is being + V3.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

She said, "I have lost my keys."
options: She said that she had lost her keys.
She said that she has lost her keys.
She said that she loses her keys.
She told that she had lost her keys.
questions.solution: Present perfect → **past perfect** (had lost); I → she; my → her. B skips the backshift; C drops two tenses; D uses 'told' without a listener.
questions.shortcut: have + V3 → had + V3 after a past reporter.

questions.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** A little knowledge is a dangerous thing. **P:** He prescribed the wrong medicine. **Q:** The patient's condition worsened. **R:** A half-trained assistant ran the clinic. **S:** The owner suspended him immediately. **6.** Better no training than half training.
questions.solution: **R** gives the half-trained assistant (the example S1 warns of) → **P** his wrong prescription → **Q** the worsening it caused → **S** the immediate suspension → S6's moral. RPQS.
questions.shortcut: Cause chain: assistant → prescription → worsening → suspension.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The scissors ___ on the table.
questions.solution: 'Scissors' is a plural-only noun (like trousers, spectacles) — it always takes a **plural** verb: 'The scissors are on the table.'
questions.shortcut: Twin-noun objects (scissors, trousers) are plural.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
options: The human body clock can be adjusted at will.
Night work cannot be abolished, so its health costs should be managed deliberately.
Night shift work should be abolished to protect workers.
Only hospital staff suffer from disturbed body clocks.
questions.solution: The passage states night work must continue ('economies cannot simply switch off') and then spends two paragraphs on softening its costs — the thesis is **manage, don't abolish**. B contradicts the passage; C narrows it wrongly; D reverses the biological finding.
questions.shortcut: Thesis lives in the pivot sentence: 'not to abolish but to soften its costs'.
questions.passage:
Modern economies run around the clock, but the human body does not. Shift workers — nurses, drivers, security guards, bakers — make up nearly a fifth of the workforce in industrialised countries, and they pay for the convenience of others with their health. Decades of research now link night shift work to disturbed sleep, weight gain, high blood pressure and even reduced resistance to infection. The reason is biological: a cluster of brain cells keeps a master clock that expects light at dawn and darkness at night. When exposure to bright light comes at midnight instead, the clock drifts out of alignment, and hormones that should rise at night rise at odd hours.

Yet economies cannot simply switch off. Hospitals, transport networks and power grids must run continuously. The sensible response, therefore, is not to abolish night work but to soften its costs. Some factories now rotate shifts forward — morning to evening to night — because forward rotation disturbs the body clock least. A few employers offer bright light during shifts and darkened rest rooms afterwards; both measurably improve alertness. Governments could help by treating shift work as a health issue, not merely a wage issue: regular medical checks, protection from arbitrary schedule changes and training in sleep hygiene would cost little.

The deeper problem is cultural. We admire the executive who answers email at 2 a.m. and mock the worker who naps. Until rest is treated as performance infrastructure — as serious as bandwidth or safety gear — the night shift will remain what it is today: the invisible subsidy that keeps the day shift comfortable.

questions.q: According to the passage, shift workers make up nearly a fifth of the workforce in —
questions.solution: The opening line fixes the figure: 'nearly a fifth of the workforce in **industrialised countries**.' The other options replace the stated scope.
questions.shortcut: Detail questions: return to the exact line and match nouns.

questions.q: It can be inferred from the passage that factories rotate shifts forward because —
options: forward rotation disturbs the body clock the least
questions.solution: The passage gives the reason in the same sentence: forward rotation is used '**because** forward rotation disturbs the body clock least.' B, C and D supply plausible but unstated motives.
questions.shortcut: Because-clause = the inference gift: quote it back.

questions.q: The phrase 'soften its costs' as used in the passage means —
options: reduce the harmful effects of night work
make night work cheaper for employers
raise the wages of night workers
questions.solution: The costs in question are the health harms listed earlier; softening them = **reducing the damage**. Wages are explicitly called insufficient ('not merely a wage issue'), and shift length is not discussed.
questions.shortcut: Replace the phrase with its context: costs = health harms.

questions.q: The author's attitude toward shift workers can best be described as —
questions.solution: The author catalogues their health costs, proposes protections and calls them an 'invisible subsidy' — concern for an unfairly burdened group, i.e. **sympathetic concern**. Mocking is attributed to culture, not to the author.
questions.shortcut: Tone = verdict on the subject: protections proposed → sympathy.
